newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK handover legislature passes civil rights curbs.
newsitem.headline: HK handover legislature passes civil rights curbs.

text.p: Hong Kong's future legislature rammed through two laws on Saturday to curb political liberties and civil rights when China takes back the 156-year-old British colony in little more than two weeks' time.
The popular Democratic Party and Governor Chris Patten's office attacked the move as a step backwards for freedom.
The Provisional Legislature met across the border in the Chinese city of Shenzhen and passed amendments to two Hong Kong laws governing freedom of association and assembly.
The changes will take effect upon the handover on July 1.
The amendments were drawn up by post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa, on a cue from Beijing's communist rulers.
A dozen or so pro-democracy activists gathered outside Tung's office in a glass tower block in Hong Kong's financial district on Saturday in protest against the moves.
Under a 1984 treaty with Britain, China promised Hong Kong could keep its capitalist way of life unchanged and enjoy great autonomy in all but military and diplomatic affairs.
But many of Hong Kong's 6.4 million people fear China will impose repressive communist-style rule, especially since the bloody 1989 anti-democracy crackdown in Beijing.
The new laws empower police to ban protests on grounds of "national security" or threats to China's territorial integrity and to disband organisations with overseas political funding.

The changes, which curtail the rights of political parties and the rights of people to stage protest marches by setting rules on prior approval, are hotly contested by Hong Kong pro-democracy groups and by western governments -- most vocally the departing colonial power Britain.
"This is a clear sign of things to come," said Democratic Party leader Martin Lee.
"These changes represent a step backwards for freedom and will revive colonial restrictions on basic rights," Lee said.
"The introduction of 'national security' leaves the laws open to interpretation and political censorship."
The changes will reverse a liberalisation that has taken place over the past five years under Patten, who relaxed strict colonial laws on political liberties.

"It's a bleak thought that this is the legislature replacing Hong Kong's legitimate, democratically elected Legislative Council in just over two weeks' time," said Patten's spokesman Kerry McGlynn. "It's a cutback in civil liberties."
He noted that Hong Kong's legal profession had branded the changes as a challenge to the rule of law in the territory.

But Michael Suen, Tung's Secretary for Policy Coordination, said at the Shenzhen session the future government, in drafting the changes, tried to strike a balance between civil liberties and social order, an argument ridiculed by the democracy camp.

The 60-member provisional legislature, packed with pro-China politicians and tycoons, was appointed by Beijing to supplant Hong Kong's elected Legislative Council when the British colony becomes an autonomous Chinese region at midnight on June 30.
Members were picked six months ago by a 400-strong selection committee tightly screened by Beijing.

The Democratic Party won the lion's share of seats in 1995 elections but faces the political wilderness on July 1 when China dissolves the legislature. It has often threatened to launch court challenges to laws passed by the provisional body.
Two pro-democracy legislators in the provisional chamber, minority voices in the assembly, tried in vain on Saturday to dilute the new legislation by proposing amendments.
